title: Understanding Lithiation Dynamics in micro-Si-C Composite Anodes by in situ Electrochemical Liquid-Cell Transmission Electron Microscopy
content: With the increasing demand for higher energy density and high-capacity electrode materials, silicon has emerged as an attractive anode material, offering more than ten times (4,200 mAh/g) the capacity of conventional graphite anodes. However, silicon undergoes significant volume expansion during lithiation, leading to severe stress evolution and particle pulverization, which ultimately results in performance degradation and a shortened lifespan [1-3]. To mitigate these challenges, deeper understanding of the fundamental mechanisms behind charge-discharge dynamics of Si-based anodes is required to achieve long-term stability and practical implementation [4]. In this regard, in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) has provided unique real-time insights into these processes, allowing direct observation of the structural and chemical changes during battery operation. [5-8] However, in situ TEM studies on Si anodes have been mainly achieved using open-cell configuration and silicon nanoparticles which are significantly different from actual battery operating conditions [5-8]. While practical Si anodes are composed of Si microparticles (Si MPs) and carbon-binder domain (CBD) to enhance the stability, charge-discharge behaviors of Si MPs and complex interplay between CBD and Si MPs remain poorly understood [9-10].
